clue.text: Rated X, an adult film includes scene of Kublai Khan's pleasure dome

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Rated X, an adult film includes scene of Kublai Khan's pleasure dome': X + AN + A(dult) + U(film) leaves a D unaccounted for; the clue is likely misread (perhaps 'an ad, U film') and no source confirms it.
annotationWithheld.clue: Rated X, an adult film includes scene of Kublai Khan's pleasure dome

clue.text: Intellectually an ally for me, not excluding love in the heart

indicators.note: something placed in the heart of a word sits in its middle, here splitting the two outer pieces

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: excluding means leaving a letter out, so the word not loses the letter for love

parts.note: taken as written before the letter is removed
love is zero in tennis scoring, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone sizes up a friend's mind, insisting love sits at its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excluding' takes O (love) out of NOT, leaving NT; 'in the heart' sets NT in the middle of ME and ALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something done by way of the mind or intellect.

clue.text: Composure shown by a philatelist is bound to impress

definitions.text: Composure shown by a philatelist is bound to impress

parts.words: Composure shown by a philatelist is bound to impress
parts.note: a stamp enthusiast's 'collectedness' is the set they have collected, kept bound in an album; to impress is to stamp

explanation.surface: A stamp collector's calm manner is certain to win admirers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composure' puns on being collected; 'bound' is the album binding; 'impress' is to stamp a mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobbyist's assembled postage pieces, usually mounted in a bound album.

clue.text: We left the Far East to find prosperity

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Emigrants quit Asia in search of a better life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Far East' looks like one place, but it splits into FAR and E (East).
explanation.definitionFit: Welfare is wellbeing, good fortune and health, a synonym for prosperity in older usage.

clue.text: Easily accessible baggage makes police investigation a doddle

explanation.surface: Luggage that opens easily turns a detective's job into child's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a suitcase that opens and closes readily; idiomatically a legal matter so clear it is resolved without effort (a doddle is British slang for an easy task).

clue.text: That's a novel finish for a trouser-leg!

definitions.text: That's a novel finish for a trouser-leg!

parts.words: That's a novel finish for a trouser-leg!
parts.note: the folded-back hem at the bottom of trousers, and also the phrase for a surprising, novel happening ('a ... for the books')

explanation.surface: A tailor remarks on an unusual hem at the bottom of some trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: British idiom: 'that's a turn-up for the books' means a surprise; a turn-up is also a trouser cuff.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuff folded upward at a trouser hem, and colloquially an unexpected surprise.

clue.text: Leo's inclined to leer at girls when he's out with the German

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of their usual order

parts.note: the name taken as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: A womaniser named Leo eyes up girls whenever he goes out with his German friend.
explanation.definitionFit: To ogle is to stare lecherously, a close synonym of leering.

clue.text: PE aids lung expansion, so don't hesitate, get into the swim

definitions.text: PE aids lung expansion, so don't hesitate, get into the swim

parts.words: PE aids lung expansion, so don't hesitate, get into the swim
parts.note: advice to dive straight into the pool, the idiom for committing boldly to something without hesitating

explanation.surface: A gym teacher urges a nervous pupil to dive into the pool for their lungs' sake.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means both to dive into water and, figuratively, to commit to a bold step.
explanation.definitionFit: To leap into water headlong, and idiomatically to commit decisively after hesitation.

clue.text: See 8
See 8
Batman gets the bird

indicators.note: gets read as 'becomes', so the hero's name turns into a new arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: The Caped Crusader is booed off stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets the bird' suggests being jeered, but 'the bird' is the definition and 'gets' the scrambling signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantam is a small breed of domestic chicken.

clue.text: Supports FA, since new reshuffle

indicators.note: a reshuffle reorders a cabinet, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Football Association has paid for things since its latest boardroom shake-up.
explanation.walkthrough: FA is the Football Association, England's football governing body.
explanation.definitionFit: To finance someone is to back them with money, a verb sense matching supports.

clue.text: Open display of emotion many are moved by it

parts.note: something open is public, done in full view
a transport is an outburst of strong feeling, as in transports of joy

explanation.surface: A public outburst of feeling stirs many onlookers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moved' looks emotional, but it means physically carried, as by buses and trains.
explanation.definitionFit: Buses, trains and trams carry great numbers of commuters each day.

clue.text: It's boring, stuck here in the mating season

explanation.surface: A wry remark that even breeding time can be dull.
explanation.definitionFit: A rut is a dull routine one is stuck in, and also the period when deer and similar animals breed.

clue.text: This chick is, like, yesterday's news

definitions.text: This chick is, like, yesterday's news

parts.words: This chick is, like, yesterday's news
parts.note: a newly hatched bird and a stale story share the same age: hatched or printed only yesterday

explanation.surface: Teen-speak dismisses a girl as passé.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chick' looks like slang for a young woman, but it is a baby bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a newborn chick and yesterday's paper have existed for just twenty-four hours.

clue.text: The pulse of India

parts.note: not a heartbeat but an edible legume, the lentils central to the subcontinent's cooking

explanation.surface: Something presented as the beating heart of the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Dal is split lentils or other legumes, a staple of South Asian cuisine.

clue.text: African tribe is first-class, won't be caught in the middle

indicators.note: being caught in the middle means sitting within another piece, here the first-class letters

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written here as AI
shan't is an old-fashioned way of saying won't

explanation.surface: A tribe is praised as excellent yet refuses to be trapped between rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be caught in the middle' sounds like a peacemaker's fear, but it is the container signal; the top-quality mark A1 is written with the numeral read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ashanti are a people of central Ghana in West Africa.

clue.text: Put feelers out to Anne about ten-acre plot

indicators.note: about signals the letters are turned round and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A land agent sounds out a woman named Anne over a ten-acre field.
explanation.definitionFit: Insects' sensory organs on the head are their feelers.

clue.text: Square and rugged, but skinny

parts.note: rugged terrain is craggy, full of rocky outcrops

explanation.surface: A description of someone stocky and weatherbeaten, yet thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Scraggy means thin and bony, a synonym of skinny.

clue.text: Conclude meetings, which may be of a tertiary nature

definitions.text: which may be of a tertiary nature

parts.note: to conclude is to close
encounters are meetings

explanation.surface: A chairman wraps up proceedings that may concern rock strata.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the film 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind': tertiary means third.
explanation.definitionFit: Spielberg's film title makes them 'of the Third Kind', and third is the meaning of tertiary.

clue.text: Chap takes an age to reach Herts town

indicators.note: read backwards from the town, the chap is what remains when the age is taken away

parts.note: Stevenage is a town in Hertfordshire (Herts), north of London
an age is AGE, taken as written

explanation.surface: A man spends forever travelling to a Hertfordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says the man plus AGE makes STEVENAGE, a town in Hertfordshire, England; so removing AGE gives the man.
explanation.definitionFit: Steven is a male first name, and a chap is a man.

clue.text: Become less severe about religious festival

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Lent is the Christian season before Easter

explanation.surface: Someone softens their stance concerning a church season.
explanation.definitionFit: To relent is to soften or yield, easing one's harshness.

clue.text: While he's not at the meeting, he's in on it

definitions.text: While he's not at the meeting, he's in on it

parts.words: While he's not at the meeting, he's in on it
parts.note: the Latin legal phrase for being dealt with while not present needs 'in' in front of it

explanation.surface: An absent colleague is nonetheless part of the plot.
explanation.walkthrough: Legal Latin 'in absentia' means in someone's absence; 'he's in on it' hints that the word follows 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'in absence', used when a matter proceeds without the person present.

clue.text: Root cause of sugar industry going under

definitions.text: Root cause of sugar industry going under

parts.words: Root cause of sugar industry going under
parts.note: not the reason for a business collapse, but a plant root, grown underground, from which sugar is extracted

explanation.surface: An analyst explains the underlying reason a sugar firm went bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Root cause' and 'going under' suggest business failure, but the plant's root is the source of sugar and grows underground.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar beet is a crop whose swollen root is refined into sugar.

clue.text: Fifty dance wildly, causing wicked inflammation

indicators.note: wildly signals that the letters are flung into disorder

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
taken as written

explanation.surface: A frenzied dance by fifty people leads to a nasty swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wicked inflammation' looks medical, but it is something with a wick that burns.
explanation.definitionFit: A candle is a wax stick with a wick that is lit to give a flame.

clue.text: Prohibition imposed on north-eastern region of Italy

indicators.note: the prohibition word is placed over and around the compass letters, enclosing them

parts.note: a veto is a ban or prohibition
NE is the abbreviation for north-east

explanation.surface: A ban is placed on an Italian region in the north-east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'north-eastern' looks like part of the definition, since Veneto is in Italy's north-east, but it gives NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Veneto is the administrative area around Venice in northern Italy.

clue.text: Back-chat at the heart of the aga-saga?

indicators.note: back means the letters picked out are read in reverse order
at the heart of means letters are taken from inside the following words

explanation.surface: Is cheeky talk the core of a middle-class novel?
explanation.walkthrough: An aga-saga is a British novel about comfortable country life (an Aga is a cooking range). SAG inside it is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Gas is informal for idle talk or chatter.

clue.text: Arnold Bennett's heroine coined it in India

explanation.surface: A literary heroine made money while living in India.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Tellwright heads Bennett's 'Anna of the Five Towns'; the anna was a former Indian coin worth a sixteenth of a rupee.
